Title: To transfer out or not to transfer out? That is the question.

Messages.Author: Aria
Messages.Body:
Hello, everybody!
I am Aria, a young player from France. I play Jyhad since 2006 and I
am used to playing some tournaments in France.
My English is not perfect, so, I apologize for the mistakes you will
find in this text.

I would like to introduce you an issue, and a solution I propose to
solve it.

Over the past few months, I have noted that tranfer out ( the fact
to kill yourself by spending your last pool, however), has a huge
influence in a game and a tournament. By killing yourself, you change
dramatically the tempo of a game, the number of actions your predator
needs to kill you, and you broke all the calculations of players who
are still alive. By transfering out, you can change all the game and
literally choose who will win, or NOT win.
Many of you are used to threating other players to kill yourself in
order to make them stop their actions. Maybe, like me, you are used to
losing games because of some players decided to transfer out, giving
victory points or game win to your prey just to annoy you or to make
you loose the game.
In the last party I played, a player decided to not transfer out and
it made me win. He was my predator and, because my prey quickly killed
her prey, in a three way configuration I fought to make my predator
survive.
I was playing a deck based on “hide the heart”, and I was able to
reduce some bleeds and intercept deflected bleeds on me. Finally, I
killed my prey and killed my predator next turn, because he has no
chance against me, and he knew it. At any time, my predator could kill
himself and allow my prey to get 2 vp and prevent me from getting the
Game Win.
In the same game, the first prey of my prey killed herself. It was
not very important but it made my prey gain an action, one more bleed
in the same turn, it could kill my predator.

I am really opposed to the rule that allows a player to choose his
death. In my opinion, that rule is a violation of the “Play To Win”
rule. That last rule has been made to prevent some random actions in a
game, and to force players to do everything they can to get the GW.
But, if they can’t get the GW, what choices do they have?
First, the PTW rule forces you to get as many vp as you can. If you
can’t get any more vp, nowadays you can do anything you want! But
there is a way to get more vp. I mean, if you survive until the time
limit, you win 0.5vp! So, why a player is allowed to kill himself?
Where is the rule allowing him to not play in order to get this last
half vp?

Another question has to be asked here. Why a player kills himself
during a game? Where is the benefit for him in suicide?
I’ve got 2 reasons. First, you do not like a player, and you want to
punish him because he is an asshole or whatever, so, you transfer
out.
The other one: you want to prevent a player in your table to make a
game win, because you know that if he does not get a game win, you
have more chances to play the final table.
Each of these two reasons is illegal and a violation of rules. The
first one contradicts the fair play, the second one contradicts the
rule, which says “you have to play each game independently of whatever
event or information out of the table”. I heard some players say “ if
your predator deserves a vp why not to give him?” Because, if he is
not able to kill you, maybe he does not deserve a victory point!

My last opinion about the suicide in V:tES, is that it forces
players to play only a few kinds of deck. I think that decks which
want to control the table, such as multi-rush decks, Z decks ( funny
decks), and some intercept decks have a huge disadvantage in
tournaments, because they cannot make their prey loose huge amounts of
pool in one turn. A multi-rush deck, for example, often kills all the
minions of his prey and his grandprey before killing them. But he
risks that his grand prey transfers out, to have her revenge. Other
control decks, like my "hide the heart" deck for example, can’t win if
a player kills himself.
The amount of pool a player can loose in one turn is about 10 : 3
vessel/blood doll, an expensive master and actions like recruit
expensive allies, and finally 4 transfer points at the end of your
turn. So, if you do not want to risk your grandprey kills herself, you
have to be able to make more than 10 pool of damage in one turn. Only
a few decks are able to make that amount of damage. So, allowing
suicide is an (one of the many) obstacle of deck diversity in
tournaments.

There is a last issue in allowing suicide: There are many ways to
defend people “cross table”, reduce bleed, boons, parity shift, eagle
sight… But there is no way to defend yourself against someone
committing suicide, giving your prey 6 pools and a victory point.

My solution? Respect the “Play To Win” rule!
“A player can’t spend his last pool point during his turn unless it
will give him a victory point or a game win”. These are the few words
I want to read in the next rulebooks. It is not perfect. I know that a
player can spend all except 1 pool point and tap all his minions and
say “next”, but it could be the first step of a rule like “a player
has to play in order to survive as long as he can”, but that is for my
secret dreams.

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:

Aria, you have made some excellent points. I had never thought about
how self-ousting hurts certain kinds of decks, particularly rush
combat decks, thus discouraging deck diversity. You are also right
that even though there are cards that allow you to control most other
aspects of the table, there is no card that allows you to prevent self-
ousting. (Life Boon might do it, but I think it would only prevent it
if the self-oust happened on the last transfer of the influence
phase.)

I mentioned in the other thread that I think it is acceptable to self-
oust in order to try to get more tournament points if you can't get
more victory points. That is another reason to do it. In the example
you gave of trying to prevent someone else from getting a game win by
self-ousting, it really does makes sense to self-oust if (and only if)
you will cause yourself and the other player to achieve a tie in the
game's final results, thus increasing your tournament points.

However, I'm not sure if playing for tournament points violates the

"you have to play each game independently of whatever event or

information out of the table" rule.

There may be countless other reasons (maximizing TPs, trying to do

artificially prevented. If you feel it's not legal call a judge.

> players to play only a few kinds of deck.

So if French players are so eager to suicide, play active decks. It's a
metagame thing. E.g. in Hungary we used to have an insane amount of
wall decks. So everybody started playing block denial or combat. Maybe
your meta needs more S&B and Powerbleed and weenie bleed/rush.

> There is a last issue in allowing suicide: There are many ways to
> defend people “cross table”, reduce bleed, boons, parity shift, eagle
> sight… But there is no way to defend yourself against someone
> committing suicide, giving your prey 6 pools and a victory point.

There are 2 very good ways. First, you can play a Boon when the player
self-ousts. But more importantly, you can ensure that people have fun
and don't feel to be in a truly lost position, and they won't be so
much inclined to self-oust.

I can't even be bothered to estimate how many games I've played in the
last 16 years, even despite being more or less dormant for the last
1-2 years, but I've self-ousted maybe 5-10 times total. I'd say,
definitely less than 1% of the games. About half of those were VP-deals
(which are now handled), so that leaves us with a really low amount of
self-ousts. It is generally not worth it to self-oust. But I still
prefer to have the option rather than be arbitrarily limited in my play.

> My solution? Respect the “Play To Win” rule!

I fully agree with this one! :)

Regards,

Daneel

I have self-ousted in a tournament situation before for strategical
reasons.
I had 2VP
My prey had 1VP
My pred had 0VP

My prey was too well setup and was binning my guys when I went
forward. I was nearly out of resources. My Pred couldn't get me
before he was gotten however, as I had a bit too much pool if I
sacked.

I rationalised that my Prey was going to get the remaining 3VP and win
the game. So I self-Ousted. My Pred got 1VP and my Prey then got my
Pred eventually. Game ended up 2-2-1.

Sometimes a noble sacrifice is the way to go.

I think it's a bit less black-and-white than that.

I think most people generally sit down to play V:tES to play V:tES (and
even get a shot at scoring some VPs or a GW), and not to self-oust after
playing for a while. Now as the game progresses, some players' chances
improve, but that is only possible by diminishing other players' chances.
Once a player has no tangible chance to win, then depending on the game
so far, he may choose from among a number of equally valid plays. Some
examples:

1. Go all-out on his prey, crippling him (and likely granting his predator
two easy VPs).
2. Pick a random target and screw his game cross-table.
3. Play on as before, and be ousted soon in the process.
4. Wall up to screw his predator and help his prey.
5. Self-oust to help his predator.

Just as you can argue that #5 is kingmaking, the end result is that no
matter which action the player chooses, he will still have in impact
on the table and on the play of others. He cannot choose one over the
other based on that; because if he chooses #3 and plays on exactly as
before, his prey might be pissed that he doesn't wall up (potentially
increasing the time he survives), and his predator can be pissed that
he doesn't go full forward, as any resources spent on defending
against him just eat up his resources to get what he practically
already has.

> Am I alone to think that it is normal to play in order to survive?

Nope. The tournament rules assume that your main incentive is to win
the game, and if you can't do that, get as many VPs as you can. If you
can't get any VPs, you can do what you want.

> I am new in the newsgroup, this is my second message, I did not know
> that subject was already debated many times, but if a lot of players
> think that we must try to set a rule against "transfer out", maybe
> they are right?

Maybe? But probably not.

The short version (which has already been covered here):

A) The number of times someone is in a truly lost position, such that
they are enabled by the rules to oust themselves is very small. Such
that it doesn't come up all that much.

B) Making a rule that outlaws self ousting by some sort of mechanical
means (i.e. "you can't spend your last pool if...") is mostly
pointless, as it is incredibly easy to circumvent in any number of
ways.

The vast majority of the time, people don't oust themselves. The vast
majority of the time, people aren't legally allowed to oust themselves
(due to the PTW rules). It just doesn't come up all that much. In the
small number of situations where someone is in a truly lost position
such that them ousting themselves is both possible and viable, it will
occasionally happen, and we can all live.

If you end up not getting a table sweep 'cause you turned your
predator into a smoking crater and they spend their last pool to spite
you and give your grand predator a VP and 6 pool, maybe next time
you'll remember not to turn your predator into a smoking crater.

-Peter

All of these things are completely true. And I agree with you here.
But to pull it back into the realm of "we don't want people to self
oust!"--if you have a deck whose sole defense against their predator
is to blast them into the stone age, then that is what you have to do.
But you should also be able to win the game while doing it, even if
your predator gets ousted 'cause you nuked them (either by their
predator or by self ousting).

As has been established, I play a lot of rush decks (well, I used to,
and don't as much anymore, but still :-) And the ones that were most
successful were the ones that:

A) Ousted my first prey quickly and brutally.
B) Survived to be the last guy at the table.

nuked their predator into a giant smoking hole. Which generally
resulted in them getting ousted. But as I was trying to back oust
them, that worked.

reliably get the VP for doing so!" Which strikes me as an unecessary
change. You can nuke your predator. But the cost is that you are
giving a VP to someone else for doing so. Which strikes me as a
completely reasonable trade off for circumventing the standard
predator>prey relationship (i.e. giving a guy *two* predators).

Honestly John, I'm not a die-hard tourney guy, so I'm probably the
wrong person to ask. Peter or Steve have far more experience than I
at such things.

BUT, from my limited experience, I do believe the tourney scene
suffers a little. I mean, yes, there are a wider variety of decks
that show up, but inevitably, unless one of those "off the wall" or
atypical decks happens to be the "Paper" to your "Rock", your greatest
concern if you get to a final table probably revolves around:

1.) stealth bleed (either of the super fast weenie type, or the
slightly less fast, but more potent, mid cap with DOM type).
2.) stealth vote
3.) breed & boon
4.) Aus wall

Going off on another tangent (to this tangent), the final table decks
I've noticed rarely have guys bigger than a 7 or 8 cap. Most of them
work on the 3-6 cap range, because it's been well proven that lower
cap guys means you can generally have more of them, which means you
can take more actions.

The exceptions of course are big caps with excellent disciplines/
abilities, like Arika, Stanislava, the Toreador AAA triplets, or Lutz.

My most recent experience was last year's Western NY NAC qualifier.
The final table consisted of:

1.) weenie Dem/Obf
2.) Tzimice wall
3.) Stanislava
4.) Aus intercept (with some eagle sight)
5.) Tre/!Tre toolbox

Steve won with his Tre/!Tre deck, but not before Ruben Feldman and his
Dem/Obf totally squashed the Tzimice and Stanislava decks. He just had
too many weenies, who all bled for 2-4 each consistently.

LSJ has done a good job of introducing more big caps with interesting
abilities, and more cards to punish weenies (Neonate breech, Scourge
of the Enochians), while helping to enable more big guy actions (Enkil
Cog), but I think there is still a ways to go.

And I think a discipline-less bounce card that isn't as poor as Lost
in Translation would be a big start. I'd love to see more decks that
could pack in a "defense module" of 6-9 bounce cards, and 2-4 delaying
tactics, and then the rest could be - ANYTHING! I think it would
definitely shake up the tourney scene for the better, but that's just
my very inexperienced $0.02.

-Asif Chaudhry

duplicate copies of my superstar 10 cap, I'm on five pool and there's
an hour left in the game and its the first round of a tournament,
transferring out allows me extra time to collect myself before the
next round, relax and regroup. Making me sit at a table for an hour
while my prey who went nuclear on the table tries to bleed through a

predator.

cause mistakes. Saying there is no benefit to escaping a no win
situation early has been demonstrated to be untrue.

kind of crazy anarch blood brothers bruise/bleed." Personally, I'd
prefer the "hard to anticipate and manipulate" meta game - it would
make creating decks to compete in such an environment much more fun
and challenging.

On May 14, 12:36 am, OldFan <asif.i.chaud...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Trying to be as clear as possible:  I'd like to see decks have viable
> "Trump" technology such as what dominate/AUS/Pre bloat has at the
> moment, which can keep you from being ousted, while not requiring you
> to block your pred's every action or torp all his guys/leave a smoking
> crater.  Thereby causing him to self-oust, just to spite you.

Are you talking about stuff like Faerie Wards that circumvents the act/
block interaction which is the spine of the game? Those kinds of cards
are super-annoying, as far as I'm concerned. Being mostly a game of
cumulative small effects, the auto-fail kinds of stuff always grates
when it crops up in VTES.

I think maybe we're just not seeing eye-to-eye in terms of what
constitutes reasonable defense. I know of plenty of decks that can
defend themselves long enough to get VPs without using bleed bounce or
Tap-n-Cap or destroying their predators utterly.

I'm also getting the sense that maybe defense just isn't an
interesting part of deck construction to you, given your comment about
how you think it would be cool if every deck could drop in the same
disciplineless defense module. I'm not going to try to tell you that
your preferences are wrong, but I certainly don't agree with them
(assuming my assessment of your preferences is correct).

> I realize that the TWDA isn't chock full of archetype/"tier 1" decks.
> But (without doing the statistical math), I would wager that a
> disproportionate number of decks in the TWDA have strong elements of
> one of those tier 1 types.  Because, well, they work.

Sure. I don't think that's avoidable, though. Some stuff is always
going to be better than other stuff. Everything else being equal
(which, thankfully, it never ever is), the better stuff is always
going to win. I'm still not seeing how that's a problem which needs a
solution, given that total equality of goodness is straight-up
impossible.

> It's HOW the "good" decks become "good".  We both agree that player
> skill accounts for quite a bit in winning.  But I would challenge you
> to give Ben Peal a crappy toolbox/Brinksmanship deck, while giving,
> say me (as an example of a bad/inexperienced player) a streamlined '94
> malk stealth bleed deck, put 3 other players at the table, and see how
> we do.

Impossible to tell with the information given. If those other three
players are all playing rush decks, and Ben's Brinksmanship deck is
one of the Enkidu varieties? Yeah, he's almost certainly going to do
better than you will.

I mean, we can make shit up at each other all day long, so let's not
do that. The point of my counterexample is that seating and player
skill are so much more important than decktype means that it's totally
possible to win with decks that don't use one of your three methods of
defense.

> My point would be:  give decks other than dom/AUS some good bounce,
> and those decks might get trotted out for NAC quals and championships
> more often.

Heh. I know you said you don't play in tournaments too much, but you
should really look at the decklists of the most recent NAC and EC. :)

> But as it stands, a "good" deck is one that plans on defending against
> being bled alot, and you do that either with dom/AUS/ or bloat
> technology.  

Or by blocking, yeah.

> Your deck doesn't do one of those 3, odds are high that it is not a "good" tournament deck.

True. And if your deck doesn't bleed well or vote well or fight well,
it's probably not good. I don't see that as a bug.

> ?
> You mean, kind of how, "Delaying Tactics" is an auto include for every
> deck that doesn't have titles or anti vote specials on their minions
> (like Gerald Windham)?
>
> Or how almost every deck in the TWDA has some kind of "untap/wake/FA/
> OtQV" cards in them.  Because sometimes you really need to have a guy
> who can do something during your pred's and/or prey's turn?
>
> You mean like that kind of auto include?

Exactly like those kinds of cards.

> Those kind of "auto-inclusions" haven't hurt the game yet.  I fail to
> see how this one would either.

They've hurt it in the sense of making it more dull, at least during
the deck-design phase of the game. Good disciplineless bounce would do
the same thing.

> Right now, the "good" decks - have some kind of solid plan on how to
> deal with bleeding, either by bounce, bloat, or intercept.  As those
> options are currently limited by discipline, I'd like to increase the
> viability of decks using designs/minions that don't necessarily focus
> on those disciplines.

Yeah, see, I'd be totally cool with disciplines that suck being given
good cards. Bleed bounce for Celerity? Great! But there's a huge
difference between giving good cards to bad disciplines and making
good disciplineless cards (even if you add a blood cost to keep allies
from playing those cards).

> It may not be possible, but it doesn't mean we shouldn't keep trying.
> If it did, LSJ wouldn't keep trying to design and print new cards that
> have been heading in the direction of "make other disciplines less bad
> when compared to dominate" and "make big cap vamps less bad when
> compared to hordes of small/mid cap vamps".
>
> And honestly, its not so much about "balance" as it is about "making
> the largest number of possible deck design/types that can win
> consistently."  So that winning has as much to do with the player/how
> the game is played as it does with what kind of deck those players are
> using.

That works for me. We are probably just disagreeing about the
particulars and specifics at this point.

> After all, to look at the thread about that degenerate "do nothing"
> deck that won brisbane 2010 recently, how deadly dull must it be to
> sit down to a game there and go "gee, I know most every deck here will
> be some kind of stealth bleed."  

Well, I think that's actually a really interesting deck, because
playing it is a really high-risk/high-reward gamble. (Note the other
people in that thread saying that they got squashed while playing
similar decks.) On top of that, I've got no interest in trying to get
other people to play more interesting decks - folks will play what
they want to, regardless of whether or not I think their decks are
cool, and that's exactly how the game should be. So I don't despair if
I honestly think that everyone around me is going to be playing
stealth/bleed, I just do my best to adapt to the environment.

> Compared to "Damn, that guy's got
> animalism/Deep song, that guy has big cap Enkil Cog shenanigans, that
> guy is doing some kind of Laibon bloat and vote, and that guy has some
> kind of crazy anarch blood brothers bruise/bleed."  Personally, I'd
> prefer the "hard to anticipate and manipulate" meta game - it would
> make creating decks to compete in such an environment much more fun
> and challenging.

Fair enough.

John Eno
